architecture-overview.text: cardano-keri gives one KERI identity a stable Cardano checkpoint while its keys rotate. KERI is Key Event Receipt Infrastructure; its AID (Autonomic Identifier) names an identity, and its KEL (Key Event Log) is the signed history of that identity's key events.
Start with Follow one identity to play registration, rotation, consumer refusal and registry uniqueness before reading the mechanisms below.

The transaction architecture — thin checkpoint, reference observers, zero-lovelace withdrawal, BLAKE3 premint — is that of the earlier deployed design (version 1). The proposed M1 registration flow below is an earlier stand-alone proposal that moves full inception admission into a repeatable attestation. It is neither the constitution's requirement (the controller's booking mint validates the inception) nor the behaviour of the model and the validators at this revision (the fold checks it); issue #559 records that conflict and its model-first repair. The proposal is not implemented; the existing BLAKE3 token proves a narrower fact. How lifecycle state is represented also changes: in version 1 it is role addresses, in the accepted design it is the datum's poison and frozen bits and its pending-termination form, read by the holding predicate. Both are described below, marked.

the-identity-plane.text: Every registered AID owns a sovereign checkpoint UTxO (unspent transaction output) carrying one AID-derived token and an inline datum with its current key state. Registration must establish both valid initial state and uniqueness; these are separate guarantees.

proposed-m1-registration-flow.text: The request need not carry the raw inception if the attestation authenticates the initial key-state projection as well as the AID. The concrete evidence carrier, reference or consumption rules, and transaction budgets remain to be specified and measured. Attestation is repeatable; checkpoint uniqueness is enforced by registry admission. There is no revival: an identity is alive until it is convicted. The registration guarantees explain the model boundaries and link the playable duplicate-registration case.

shipped-v1-evidence-flow.text: The existing implementation splits out the hash check only. Registration still receives the full inception evidence and performs the remaining admission checks; it has no registry absence check.
In this shipped flow, the parts have deliberately narrow jobs:
KERI produces the identity events, controller signatures, and witness receipts.
The BLAKE3 premint policy proves that inception bytes bind to the AID and mints a short-lived fact token.
The thin checkpoint validator protects the token, value, exact input, and unique successor.
Reference observers validate large KERI evidence through a zero-lovelace withdrawal in the same transaction.
The checkpoint UTxO is the current Cardano projection. A rotation spends it and creates its next version; no shared root or inclusion proof is needed for the key state.

stable-identity-changing-authority.text: In version 1 the checkpoint token's asset name is derived from the qualified KERI AID; in the accepted design the checkpoint holds the registry's representative asset for the AID. That policy ID and asset name form the stable Cardano handle. The datum changes as KERI rotates. In the earlier deployed design it was nine fields of pure key state:
CESR is KERI's compact encoding format. toad is the threshold of accountable duplicity: the number of witness receipts required by the event.

An indexer may locate a candidate UTxO by policy and asset name, but it does not establish authority. A consuming Cardano transaction must revalidate the exact policy and quantity-one asset, an accepted checkpoint script and version, the expected AID and a well-formed datum, and its own authorization rule. A stale index result points to a spent input and fails; an indexer outage can block discovery, but cannot create false authority.

earlier-deployed-design-role-addresses.text: State is carried by the script role address the token sits at, not by a caller-controlled status field:

In that design there was no conviction role: conviction burned the AID token and created no successor, so a consumer met the no-candidate case. That follows from the projection law — the chain never originates identity state, and no key event says "this AID is dead" for a validator to project.

under-the-accepted-design-the-poison-bit.text: Under the accepted design: the poison bit, the frozen bit and the age.
The three roles go. What replaces them is smaller and reads directly off the checkpoint a consumer already resolves:

Nothing there is a flag a caller can set: the poison and frozen bits change only by the validated steps, and the rest are facts about the output and when the checkpoint was born. The holding predicate is: authenticated context, output at the checkpoint credential, exactly one representative asset, a datum that names the expected AID, state present, unfrozen and unpoisoned, and born_at + W ≤ now. The payment's own signature is checked separately.

uniqueness-the-one-shared-object.text: In the earlier deployed design there was none. Registration uses no absence proof, so more than one candidate checkpoint can exist for an AID and a consumer cannot prove otherwise.

The accepted design adds exactly one shared structure, and confines it to the narrowest possible job: a registry mapping each AID to absent, active or permanently retired. A registration must prove absence before inserting, preventing a second first-registration of that AID. A live checkpoint keeps the token and the active key until it is convicted. Conviction first enters pending custody; only its associated consuming Registry fold burns the token and retires the key. See the registration guarantee. Rotate, poison, freeze and top-up leave the key active, and consumers do not use an active key alone as authority.

It is a registry of 32-byte keys, not a record of events — the record tree and its cursor are retired. Its mechanics are the MPFS cage — a Merkle Patricia Forestry store whose every update passes through one validator — made permissionless: requests are independent UTxOs that a booker submits (the controller, in the constitution's terms) and anyone in the folder role applies in batches (ruling D-037). It is built today in singular and runs on a development network; what is delivered and what remains is on where the registry is built. A stalled registry delays registrations and forges nothing.

transaction-architecture.text: The checkpoint is intentionally small. In the shipped operation flow, heavy KERI verification runs in operation-specific observer reference scripts:

The observer families shipped today are the lifecycle observer for Register, the advance observer for rotations and ARMED responses, and the enforcement observer for Freeze. The accepted design removes the third: observer_advance verifies the evidence for both an advance and a freeze — they present the same rotation and differ only in effect — and checkpoint_register dispatches that effect.

The scripts are stored in reference-script outputs; copying them inline would exceed the transaction-size limit. See Observer architecture for the wire shape, the BLAKE3 fact token, sizes and costs — including the three bytes of headroom of the version 1 observer_advance that made every datum decision a measured one.

For the proposed registration flow, the heavy inception admission moves to the earlier attestation transaction. The fold must still authenticate that result and couple registry insertion, checkpoint mint and output validation. This changes where registration evidence is checked; it does not remove those checks or change rotation evidence into inception attestations. At this revision the fold checks the inception; the constitution requires the controller's booking to do so, and issue #559 records the conflict.

permissionless-does-not-mean-unauthentic.text: In the accepted design, advance and freeze may be submitted by anyone: the evidence they present is public, the key state a rotation installs is the one that evidence establishes, and the submitter names the payee; a rotation carries a deposit only when the owner's new keys have signed its intent. A top-up may be submitted by anyone with a clear top-up mark and at least P, with no evidence and no payee. A registration is booked in the controller's role and folded by the registry's folder, a role of Singular's registry that knows nothing of KERI (constitution, principle XII); the model names no signer for either step. A poison needs the current key quorum's authorization, and a conviction needs a commitment opened beforehand. The submitter cannot change the new keys, thresholds and witnesses: they come from the rotation evidence, which the model takes as a premise and requires only to be for a strictly greater sequence number.

Where authority is needed, it is a signature over exactly the thing being decided. In the M1 V1 release, close bound the refund address in a message the current controllers signed; ckeri no longer offers that close.

Under the design ruled on 2026-09-02/03 (D-036 to D-040; the model is lean/CardanoKeri/Checkpoint.lean, the play is the checkpoint simulation) there is no owner exit: no close, no parking and no revival; a checkpoint is alive until it is convicted (#493). The current keys keep exactly one Cardano power, the poison. An identity is active, pending conviction, or convicted after the associated Registry fold. A deposit is signed by the keys of the epoch the rotation opens — so a relayer landing a public rotation can never unfreeze the owner. The refund address is chosen by whoever pays the registration and no step ever changes it.

current-boundary-and-future-planes.text: The repository proves the identity-plane rungs on a protocol-11 development network and on preprod. It does not yet show the accepted design's machine settled on a public network (the source tree implements only part of it: there is no poison spend), real three-of-seven GLEIF-scale settlement, a production deployment or mainnet service, a vLEI credential-chain verifier, a credential revocation mirror, or a wallet-to-Cardano authorization product.

The credential verifier, revocation state, value-cage authorization and wallet integration remain later layers. They consume the checkpoint as a reference input; they are not part of the identity story itself.
